items.scenario: You open Notation Hero in Sydney and use the 'Privacy choices' link to choose 'No, send nothing'. Months later the site starts sending visit counts to a second place, so the question changes. You return. items.whats_wrong: The spec says a saved answer carries a `version` so that a changed question can be asked again, but it does not say what an answer from an older version allows. For the popup to ask again in Europe, such an answer must count as no answer. With no answer, the time zone decides, and outside Europe that means everything starts with no popup. So the first change to the question silently changes every saved 'No' and 'Report errors only' outside Europe into full tracking. That undoes, on this one path, round 1's rule that an answer holds in every time zone.

items.whats_wrong: The spec says the plan builds the full list 'from the IANA time-zone database' but not from which table. A list built from the newer table therefore misses those EU and EEA (European Economic Area) visitors, who would be tracked without being asked, against G3 (Europe is asked first), and it asks unrelated countries instead.

(1) Before an answer, the wait after 'Yes' should be for a sentinel error thrown after the click, as the Sentry spec's rule does, not for any session envelope: in a broken build, Sentry already sent its visit ping at start-up and a second start does nothing, so a wait for 'a session envelope' returns at once, before the earlier error's report may have arrived. (2) The 'also after a reload' check has the same gap, so after 'No' the test reloads twice: the second reload is the moment for the first reloaded page. A broken build then fails every time instead of passing every time.

The spec keeps the `?` part on purpose to tell where a visitor came from (lines 240-241). Spike: after a client-side change from `/?utm_source=probe#frag` to `/play`, `performance.getEntriesByType('navigation')[0].name` still returns the landing address in Chromium 149, Firefox 148 and WebKit 26.5, `#frag` included, so dropping the `#` part is required, not optional. `document.referrer` is unchanged, so a visit with a referring site still shows as a referral; only the campaign tags and the landing page are lost. That the first page view then carries `/play` is reasoned from how Google's script reads the address; it was not run (untested), because the spike could not use Google's real script here. The folded residual (outside Europe, a click on Play before the load event) stays (untested) for the same reason: downloading Google's public script for a local test was refused by this session's permission check.
items.contradicts: Option 1: none. Checked: G5 (in Europe nothing loads until the visitor answers), because the address is read only after the answer, from the browser's own record; section 4's 'never the `#` part', which the text keeps; section 4's 'Page views', which already plans a page view sent from our code as a fallback; Known limits' 'Nothing from before an answer is reported in Europe' (line 533) and the privacy notice's 'In Europe nothing is sent until you answer' (lines 360-361), which stay true because the landing page view is sent after the answer. One open point: round 1's click-ID redaction (commit 734f00e5) relies on a Google setting for page addresses, and whether it covers an address set from our code is not checked. Option 2: none.

spike.what: A tiny local page served by Node's http module; every other request blocked. Open `/?utm_source=probe#frag` with a referrer, make a client-side page change to `/play` (`history.pushState`, as a Next.js link does), then read the navigation record, the address and `document.referrer`. Run in Chromium 149, Firefox 148 and WebKit 26.5.
spike.result: All three engines: the address is `/play`; the navigation record still reads `/?utm_source=probe#frag` (one record); `document.referrer` is unchanged (WebKit shortens it to the referring site's origin). Not run (untested): Google's script itself, so neither the first page view's address nor the fix's order of two page views was seen. Downloading Google's public script for a local test was refused by this session's permission check.

items.scenario: A newsletter link with a campaign tag brings you to Notation Hero in Berlin. The question waits at the bottom, but you click Play first and answer 'Yes' on the player page. Google Analytics records your visit as starting on the player page. The home page and the newsletter's tag are never sent, so the visit shows as coming from nowhere, or at best from the site that linked you.
items.whats_wrong: In Europe, Google Analytics starts only at the answer. The card does not block the page and stays through client-side page changes, so clicking Play before answering is likely the common path (reasoned, not measured). Google's script then reads the current address, `/play`: the landing page and its campaign tags are never sent, although the spec keeps the `?` part exactly to tell where a visitor came from. For these visitors the source reads as a referral or as direct, and the funnel loses its first step. No section mentions this skew.

options.label: Option 1: send the landing page after a late Yes
options.what: When the answer comes after a client-side page change, `startAnalytics()` first sends a page view for the address the visit began at, read after the answer from the browser's navigation record without its `#` part, then the one for the current page. A new Berlin end-to-end case and a plan-time check.
pros: Keeps goal 1 (who comes, and where they came from) true for visitors in Europe, on the path the non-blocking card invites.
Keeps the funnel's first two steps for them.
The browser part is checked in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, and nothing is read or kept before the answer.
cons: One more path in the loader, beside an unchecked one: client-side page views are not yet seen working with the real property (section 8, step 6).
How Google's script orders the two page views is unchecked: the `config` command sends its own page view, which this path must withhold.
Events from before the answer (a file opened, Play pressed) are still lost; only the landing page view comes back.
Whether Google's click-ID redaction covers an address set from our code is unchecked.
options.cost: About ten lines in `start.ts`, one unit case, one end-to-end case, one plan-time check against the real property.

after.text: - **A late "Yes":** a visitor in Europe may click Play before answering. When the answer comes after a client-side page change, `startAnalytics()` first sends a page view for the address the visit began at, read after the answer from the browser's navigation record (`performance.getEntriesByType('navigation')[0].name`) without its `#` part, then the one for the current page. Without it, the first page view is `/play`, and the landing page and its campaign tags never reach Google Analytics.

after.text: Land on `/?utm_source=probe`, click Play, then answer "Yes": the queue holds a page view for `/?utm_source=probe` before the one for `/play`.
- That after a late "Yes" the landing page view can come first (the `config` command's own page view withheld on that path), and that page views on later client-side page changes still arrive.

options.label: Option 2: accept it and record it in Known limits
options.what: No code change. One Known-limits line says that a late "Yes" in Europe loses the landing page and its campaign tags.
pros: No new code, and nothing more to check against the real property.
Honest: the skew is written where the numbers are explained.
The site has no visitors yet; it can switch to option 1 later if visitors in Europe matter.
cons: Visitors in Europe who play first lose their campaign source, against the spec's own reason for keeping the `?` part.
The funnel misses its first step for them, and the reports do not show that anything is missing.

after.text: - **A late "Yes" loses where the visit began.** A visitor in Europe who clicks Play before answering is counted from `/play` on: the landing page and its campaign tags are never sent, so Google Analytics shows the visit as a referral or as direct, and the funnel misses its first step.

items.recommendation: Option 1. G7 (the popup is a floating card that never blocks the player) makes 'play first, answer later' likely the common path in Europe. On that path the spec's own reason for sending the `?` part, telling where a visitor came from, fails silently. The browser part is checked in three engines, and the code is small.
items.flip_condition: Choose option 2 if the plan-time check shows Google's script cannot take the landing page view first without losing later page views, or if leocaseiro does not expect to share tagged links with visitors in Europe at launch.
items.proposed_fix: Choose between sending the landing page view after a late 'Yes' (option 1) and recording the loss in Known limits (option 2).
items.why_it_works: Option 1: the browser keeps the landing address in its navigation record after client-side page changes (checked in three engines), so it can be read after the answer and sent first, which restores the campaign source without reading or keeping anything before consent. Option 2: the limit is written down where the numbers are explained, so no one reads the Europe sources as complete.
items.clear_fix: no: a scope and trade-off choice (new loader behaviour against a recorded limit).

items.central_claim_check: Checked the spec and ran a spike. The stop that the instruction for NH-349 (the 'Privacy choices' link) prescribes, the ga-disable switch plus no more events, runs only in the tab where the answer changes (lines 507-512). The popup's Details opens the privacy notice in a new tab (lines 186-189), and the notice carries 'Change your answer at any time' with the link (line 361). Spike: from a player tab, a link with `target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"` opened `/privacy`; that tab wrote `notation-hero.privacy-choice`. The player tab received a `storage` event with the key and the new value, and the writing tab received none, in Chromium 149, Firefox 148 and WebKit 26.5. So a second tab keeps sending to Google Analytics, and after a 'No' to Sentry, until it is closed or reloaded; the browser's own signal is enough to stop it.
items.contradicts: none. It extends the instruction's own 'for the rest of the visit' to every tab; it uses section 2's storage key (line 147); and it fits F-21's change (both answers stop Google Analytics), because it stops whatever the new answer no longer allows.

spike.what: A tiny local page; every other request blocked. A player tab opens the notice through a new-tab link, the notice tab saves a new answer, and both tabs record `storage` events. Chromium 149, Firefox 148, WebKit 26.5.
spike.result: In all three engines the player tab heard the change (key `notation-hero.privacy-choice`, new value `{"choice":"none","version":1}`); the notice tab heard nothing of its own write.

items.scenario: You said 'Yes' and have a song open in one tab. From another tab, the privacy notice, you change your answer to 'No'. The song tab is never told. Google Analytics, and Sentry too, keep receiving from it until you close or reload that tab.
items.whats_wrong: The instruction for the 'Privacy choices' link says the change must stop Google Analytics 'for the rest of the visit', but the stop it describes runs only in the tab where the answer changes. The site's design makes a second tab likely: the popup's Details opens the privacy notice, which carries the link, in a new tab beside the player. The browser already tells every other open tab of the site when the saved answer changes, so the same stop can run there. A small, cheap gap; recommended as one sentence for that ticket.

before.text: (absent — added after the bullet's last sentence: "The link must also close Sentry for the rest of the visit.")

after.text: The stop also runs in every other open tab of the site: each tab listens for the `storage` event on `notation-hero.privacy-choice` and stops whatever the new answer no longer allows. NH-349's test opens two tabs, changes the answer in one, and proves no hit follows from the other.

items.proposed_fix: Add one sentence to the instruction for the 'Privacy choices' link: other open tabs listen for the browser's storage signal on the saved answer and run the same stop; the link's test covers two tabs.
items.why_it_works: All tabs of the site share one saved answer, and the browser signals every other tab when it changes (checked in three engines, also for a tab opened through a new-tab link). Running the same stop on that signal makes 'for the rest of the visit' true in every tab.
items.clear_fix: no: it adds scope to the 'Privacy choices' ticket (a second-tab stop and test). Small, but a scope choice.

items.central_claim_check: Checked the sources. The Sentry spec (PR #191, the Sentry pull request), Known limits, lines 740-742: 'Ad-blocked visitors. Their reports never arrive (D3). How many are missed is not measured: this project counts no visits outside Sentry, and adding a counter is the usage tracking NH-52 owns.' (There, D3 is the Sentry spec's decision not to bypass ad blockers, and NH-52 is the later ticket for service goals.) The 2026-06-20 spike, docs/spikes/2026-06-20-clean-slate-infra-tooling-app-skeleton.md:295, opens a decision to revisit Google Analytics (PostHog, or CloudFront logs read with Athena) 'when undercount bites'; its line 29 expects a '15–50% adblock undercount on a dev-skewed audience'. This spec names three causes (ad blockers, line 525; Europe before an answer, the table's last row, line 120; Safari's seven-day reset, lines 526-530) but no way to size them. Sentry's visit count, the only other count, misses the same blocked visitors and, in Europe, the same unanswered ones, so it cannot serve as the gauge. After this ticket the Sentry spec's reason ('counts no visits outside Sentry') is no longer literally true, but its conclusion still holds. A server-side count, such as Vercel's own request numbers, might serve as a rough ceiling (untested; not in this design).
items.contradicts: none. A Known-limits line changes no behaviour. It follows the Sentry spec's own "not measured" line and the Safari line round 1 added (commit 46b9b3b5).

spike.why: A measurement gap with nothing to run. No gauge exists in the design; checking a server-side count would need the production deployment.

items.scenario: You launch Notation Hero and share it. A month later Google Analytics shows 40 visitors. You cannot tell whether 40 people came, or 200 came and most were hidden: by ad blockers, by never answering the question in Europe, or by Safari forgetting them after a week. Nothing else counts visits, so the numbers cannot tell you when it is time to move to another tool.
items.whats_wrong: The spec documents three causes of undercounting but no way to size them, and the only other count, Sentry's, misses the same visitors. Early numbers therefore cannot tell little interest from a large uncounted share, and the 2026-06-20 plan to revisit Google Analytics 'when undercount bites' has no signal to act on. Recommended: one Known-limits line, so whoever reads the numbers knows what they cannot show.

before.text: (absent — new bullet after the Safari line, which ends: "The saved answer goes too: a visitor in Europe is asked again, and one elsewhere who said "No" through NH-349's link is counted again.")

after.text: - **How many go uncounted is not measured.** Ad blockers, visitors in Europe who never answer, and Safari's seven-day reset all shrink the counts, and Sentry's visit count, the only other one, misses the same blocked and unanswered visitors. So low numbers cannot tell little interest from a large uncounted share.

items.proposed_fix: Add one Known-limits line that says the size of the undercount is not measured and what that means for reading the numbers.
items.why_it_works: It tells whoever reads the numbers what they cannot conclude, in the same words the Sentry spec uses for ad-blocked visitors, at no cost. Building a real gauge would be usage counting outside these tools, which the Sentry spec leaves to NH-52 (the later service-goals ticket).
items.clear_fix: no: optional. It records a limit; whether to add it is leocaseiro's call, not a correction.
